cues.text: In this town, I was the only one who was not a monster.
My mum was a zombie.
My dad was a skeleton.
And I was a boy they found in a basket.
Our neighbour Hiss was a creeper. He loved hugs. Nobody wanted one.
The postman was an enderman. You could not look at him,
so we all signed for our parcels with our eyes shut.
The school bus was a slime. You got in. You got out wet.
School was me, some zombies, and two creepers.
The teacher was an enderman. So nobody ever looked at the board.
Every monster stayed out of the sun. The sun burned them.
It did not burn me. So I played outside alone.
They ate grey stew. I could not even smell it.
They could see in the dark. I walked into doors.
I was the only one of me there was.
Then there was Mo.
Mo was a zombie with a straw hat, and a scarf up to his nose.
He lived by himself at the end of the street, and he never said a word.
He just looked at me. A bit too long.
I thought he did not like humans.
One day I was on the wall, in the sun, hiding my stew in a bush.
Mo sat down next to me. In the sun.
He did not burn. "It is the hat," he said.
Then he took out a loaf of bread, and broke it in half.
No zombie eats bread. I did not ask. I was too hungry.
After that, we sat on that wall every day.
He could not see in the dark either. He carried a lantern, like me.
He got cold at night, like me.
He even sneezed. Monsters do not sneeze.
He showed me how to fish, and how to whistle,
and I showed him how to laugh, which he had forgotten.
He was the only monster who was like me. I never asked myself why.
There was one rule. At sunset, the whole village walked me home.
Then they locked my door. From the outside.
I thought it was because I was the weak one.
Even Mo stood there and watched them do it.
One night, I had had enough.
I went out of the window.
I wanted to see what they did without me.
They were not doing anything.
They were standing in a ring around my house. All of them.
And they were facing out.
They did it every night. They had done it since the basket.
Then I saw why. There were torches on the hill.
Players. With swords.
They had come to clear the village.
"Monsters!" one shouted. "Get them all!"
They came down the hill fast.
My dad lost an arm, picked it up, and bonked a man with it.
The bus sat on three of them.
The postman put one at the top of a tree.
And Hiss shook, and went white, trying so hard not to go off.
Nobody was hurt. And we were losing.
Then they knocked my mum over in the dirt.
And I thought: they are players. I look like a player.
I was the only thing in that village they would not touch.
So I ran. Under a sword, over the bus, through my dad's legs,
and I stood in front of my mum with my arms out.
"Stop! I live here! This is my family!"
It went quiet. A big player looked down at me.
"It is a trick," he said. "It is one of them, dressed up."
And he lifted his sword.
I shut my eyes.
It did not land.
Mo was there. He had caught the sword in his bare hand.
And his hand was bleeding. Red.
Zombies do not bleed red.
He pulled the scarf down.
He wiped his cheek with his sleeve, and the green came off.
There was skin under it. Skin like mine.
"Do not look so surprised," he said. "I am human too."
The bread. The lantern. The sneeze. The sun.
He had not been looking at me because he hated humans.
"Who do you think carried the basket here?" he said.
The big player took one step back. He knew that face.
"You," he said. "The player who ran away to live with monsters."
They had not come for the village. They had come for him.
Every player was staring at Mo. Not one of them looked behind.
My dad tapped one on the shoulder. With the arm he was not wearing.
The bus rolled through the rest like a bowling ball.
And Hiss only had to say one word. "Hug."
They dropped their swords and ran for the hill.
Then the whole village came out. Every zombie. Every skeleton. Every kid from my school.
Mo stood in the middle, with his hat in his hands. He did not look up.
He had lied to them for years. He thought they would hate him too.
My mum walked up to him. And put the hat back on his head.
"We always knew," she said. "Zombies do not eat bread."
Then something blew up in the forest.
Players. Not ten of them. Hundreds, pouring out of the trees.
"Run," Mo said. "East, past the pond. I dug a hideout for you, years ago."
So we ran. Everybody ran.
At the last house, I looked back. Mo was not with us.
He was standing in the street. Alone.
He put on an iron helmet. An iron chestplate. And he drew a sword.
Like and subscribe for part two.
